title: Beyond Praise: Why the Best Leaders Use Higher Forms of Recognition
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership challenges the reflexive use of praise as the primary form of recognition. When a team member shows improvement—closing a knowledge gap, leveling up a skill, hitting a milestone—a leader's instinct is to praise: 'Great job!' But praise is surface-level and short-lived. The best leaders use higher forms of recognition: they get curious about how the improvement happened, ask what obstacles the person overcame, and publicly name the specific actions and mindset shifts that made the difference. This shift from praise to appreciation deepens learning and builds real connection. It signals to the team that growth is about deliberate work, not innate talent, and it gives others a blueprint for improvement. The article shows how 'beyond praise' recognition works: a leader notices improvement and asks, 'How did you approach this differently this time?' or 'What did you learn from that failure?' The conversation becomes an asset to the whole team because the leader recognizes the person publicly, naming the process not just the result. This creates a culture where growth is visible, learnable, and valued. Praise says 'you did good'; curiosity-driven recognition says 'here is how you did good, here is what that required of you, and here is what the rest of us can learn.' It is the difference between fleeting positive feeling and lasting identity shift.

When leaders get curious about improvement ('How did you approach this differently?'), they uncover and model the deliberate practices that matter.

The best leaders shift from 'great job' to 'tell me about your thinking' and 'here is what I noticed about your approach'—and they do this publicly.
